en: A large language model is a neural network
language model in the end,
typically using the so-called transformer
architecture, which is just a special form
of neural network, you could say.
The idea behind a large language model is
that it takes text as input and spits out
text as output. Simple as that in a
nutshell.
Now, you can take that logic and build quite
complex systems on top of it because, for
example, you can replicate a thinking
process of a human because if you think
about something, that's in the end also just
you spitting out text even though you may be
not saying it aloud, but you're just
producing text in the end if you're thinking
about something. And therefore you can
replicate this with a large language model.
And therefore that's why this is such a
popular technology. It allows us to do quite
complex things because we can replicate that
thinking process. But in a nutshell,
technically, it's text in, text out.
Or specifically, it's actually tokens in,
tokens out. And that's just the mechanism by
which text is split up.
The large language models
were trained based on data where
text was used, essentially the entire
internet data and text and even some books
and so on were used. And that text was
broken apart not in words, but instead in
tokens. Tokens where some tokens represent
entire words and some tokens are parts of
words. And that was used to
model the relation between these different
words or word parts, between these different
tokens to understand how text is
formed and how different text pieces are
related.
That's why this quite granular token
approach was used to be able to model
complex relations.
This is especially easy to understand, I
think, if we, for example, look at a long
number.
If we tried to train a model
on that one long number as input,
we would quite likely not capture all
possible numbers out there in the wide world
during training, and hence we would be
producing a model that's quite bad at
numbers.
If we instead split this up into tokens, we
can understand the relations between these
numbers and how they work together, even in
different languages because we combine that
with all the other text we have, which of
course represents different languages.
And suddenly we have a model that's quite
good at working with numbers.
And that's why large language models are so
good at understanding text, at translation,
writing code, extracting information,
summarizing text, reasoning, as I mentioned,
but also tasks like classification or making
decisions
which tools they should use for certain
tasks. If you give them certain tools, which
is something AI agents and harnesses do,
which are terms we'll get back to.
